meta.titre: Kinetic energy: from the formula to work, collisions and stopping distances

sections.contenu_markdown: A bush taxi travelling at 100 km/h on the road from Yaounde to Douala carries four times as much kinetic energy as the same taxi at 50 km/h, and that is why the stopping distance at the higher speed is so much longer. Kinetic energy links speed to danger, to fuel cost and to the damage done when something is struck. At the GCE you must use the formula correctly, connect it to work done by forces, and say what the energy becomes when a moving body is brought to rest. Questions often hide the idea in a short description of a hammer, a vehicle or a collision, so the principle matters more than any single formula.

items: Work done by a constant force along its direction of motion is $W = Fs$.
Momentum is $p = mv$ and, in a collision of an isolated system, total momentum is conserved.
Gravitational potential energy near the Earth's surface changes by $\Delta E_p = mg\,\Delta h$, with $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
Energy is never created or destroyed; it is transferred from one form to another.

sections.titre: Kinetic energy, the work-energy principle and energy transformations

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked whether kinetic energy is conserved in an impact.
variantes.contenu_markdown: In every collision of an isolated system, **momentum** is conserved. In an **elastic** collision kinetic energy is also conserved (the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach); in an **inelastic** collision some kinetic energy becomes internal energy and sound. In a **perfectly inelastic** collision the bodies move off together. Example: a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ trolley moving at $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ sticks to a stationary $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ trolley. Momentum gives $v = \dfrac{2.0 \times 3.0}{3.0} = 2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The kinetic energy falls from $9.0\ \mathrm{J}$ to $6.0\ \mathrm{J}$, so $3.0\ \mathrm{J}$ has been transformed.

variantes.nom: Kinetic energy and speed on a graph
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to compare energies at different speeds.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Because $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2$, a graph of $E_k$ against $v$ is a parabola and a graph of $E_k$ against $v^2$ is a straight line through the origin with gradient $\tfrac12 m$. A change of speed from $u$ to $v$ changes the energy by a factor $(v/u)^2$; to double the energy the speed must be multiplied by $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$, not by $2$.

sections.contenu_markdown:
The **kinetic energy** of a body of mass $m$ moving at speed $v$ is the energy it has because of its motion:

$$E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2$$

with $E_k$ in joules when $m$ is in kilograms and $v$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. It is a scalar and is never negative. Because $E_k \propto v^2$, doubling the speed multiplies the energy by four, and tripling it multiplies it by nine. Using $p = mv$ gives the useful alternative form

$$E_k = \frac{p^2}{2m}$$

so for a given momentum the lighter body has the greater kinetic energy.

**Work-energy principle.** The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W_{net} = \Delta E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2 - \tfrac12 mu^2$. For a body brought to rest by a constant resisting force $F$ over a distance $s$, $Fs = \tfrac12 mu^2$, so the stopping distance is $s = \dfrac{mu^2}{2F}$ and is proportional to $u^2$.

**Where does the energy go?** Kinetic energy is not lost; it is transformed. When a moving body is stopped by friction, a collision or an impact, the kinetic energy becomes **internal energy** (increased random motion of molecules, a rise in temperature), together with some **sound**, and some work done in permanently deforming the materials involved. For example, when a fast-moving heavy object strikes a stationary one and drives into it, the kinetic energy is converted mainly into internal (thermal) energy of both objects, sound energy and the work done in deforming or displacing the material, not into more kinetic energy of the struck object alone.

**Conservation with gravity.** For a body moving without resistance, $E_k + E_p$ stays constant. If a resisting force does work $W_{res}$, then $E_{k,final} = E_{k,initial} + mg\,\Delta h_{fall} - W_{res}$.

etapes.justification: The work done by the braking force removes all of the kinetic energy, so $Fs = E_k$.
The force gives a constant deceleration $a = F/m$; then use $t = v/a$.
Kinetic energy increases by $2^2 = 4$, so the distance with the same force also increases fourfold.

sections.enonce_markdown: A taxi of mass $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is brought to rest by brakes that exert a constant resisting force of $6.0\ \mathrm{kN}$. Find its kinetic energy, the braking distance, the braking time, and the braking distance if the initial speed were $40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ with the same force.
sections.conclusion_markdown: The taxi stops in $40\ \mathrm{m}$ in $4.0\ \mathrm{s}$. At twice the speed the stopping distance is $160\ \mathrm{m}$, four times as long. The $240\ \mathrm{kJ}$ of kinetic energy becomes internal energy of the brakes, tyres and road.

items.pourquoi_faux: The speed is squared in the formula, so the energy becomes four times larger.
items.erreur_markdown: Doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy.
items.correction_markdown: $E_k \propto v^2$; for double the energy multiply the speed by $\sqrt2$.

items.pourquoi_faux: The joule requires kilograms and metres per second; other units give a wrong numerical answer.
items.erreur_markdown: Using the mass in grams, or the speed in $\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$, in $\tfrac12 mv^2$.

items.pourquoi_faux: Only the speed is squared. Squaring the momentum as well gives a quantity with the wrong dimensions.
items.correction_markdown: Write $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2$, or $E_k = p^2/2m$ if momentum is given.

items.pourquoi_faux: Total energy is conserved; the kinetic energy is converted to internal energy, sound and deformation.
items.erreur_markdown: Saying that kinetic energy is lost and disappears in an impact.
items.correction_markdown: Name the forms of energy produced, such as heating of the bodies and sound.

items.pourquoi_faux: Momentum is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.
items.erreur_markdown: Assuming kinetic energy is conserved whenever momentum is conserved.
items.correction_markdown: Use conservation of momentum to find the speeds, then compare kinetic energies before and after to classify the collision.

items.enonce_markdown: A footballer kicks a ball of mass $0.45\ \mathrm{kg}$ so that it leaves the boot at $18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Calculate its kinetic energy and the speed at which the same ball would have twice this kinetic energy.
items.solution_markdown: $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12 (0.45)(18)^2 = $ **$73\ \mathrm{J}$** (72.9 J). For twice the energy, $v^2$ must double, so $v = 18\sqrt{2} = $ **$25.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**, not $36\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

items.enonce_markdown: A bullet of mass $20\ \mathrm{g}$ travelling at $400\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ embeds itself in a fixed block of wood and comes to rest after penetrating $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$. Calculate its initial kinetic energy and the average resisting force, and state into what form the kinetic energy is mainly converted.
items.solution_markdown: With $m = 0.020\ \mathrm{kg}$, $E_k = \tfrac12 (0.020)(400)^2 = $ **$1.6\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$**. By the work-energy principle $Fs = E_k$, so $F = \dfrac{1600}{0.10} = $ **$1.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N}$**. The energy becomes mainly internal (thermal) energy of the bullet and the wood, with some sound and the work of deforming the wood.

items.enonce_markdown: A car of mass $800\ \mathrm{kg}$ with its engine off starts from rest and rolls down a straight slope of length $380\ \mathrm{m}$, falling through a vertical height of $25\ \mathrm{m}$. The resistive forces do $7.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$ of work. Calculate (a) its kinetic energy at the bottom, (b) its speed there, (c) the average resistive force on the slope, and (d) the distance it travels on a level road before stopping if the brakes then apply a constant force of $4.0\ \mathrm{kN}$ and other resistive forces are ignored. ($g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$)
items.solution_markdown: (a) Loss of potential energy $= mgh = 800 \times 9.8 \times 25 = 1.96\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$. Then $E_k = 1.96\times10^{5} - 7.6\times10^{4} = $ **$1.2\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$**. (b) $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_k}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.2\times10^{5}}{800}} = \sqrt{300} = $ **$17\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**. (c) $F = \dfrac{W}{s} = \dfrac{7.6\times10^{4}}{380} = $ **$2.0\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{N}$**. (d) $s = \dfrac{E_k}{F} = \dfrac{1.2\times10^{5}}{4.0\times10^{3}} = $ **$30\ \mathrm{m}$**.

items_markdown: Kinetic energy is $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2 = p^2/2m$; it is a scalar and proportional to the square of the speed.
Work-energy principle: net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy, so stopping distance $s = mu^2/2F$.
When a moving body is stopped, its kinetic energy is transformed into internal energy, sound and deformation; energy as a whole is conserved.
Momentum is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.
Use SI units (kg, $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$) and convert $\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ by dividing by $3.6$ before using the formula.
